Physics: The section spreads sensibly across mechanics, electromagnetism, optics and modern physics, and almost all keys and numerical data check out (Q3, 7, 18, 26, 27, 28, 31 are correctly computed with sensible distractors). Difficulty is skewed toward single-formula recall, with only Q18, Q27 and Q31 demanding genuine multi-step work, so a couple of the easiest items could be upgraded to restore BITSAT-level challenge. The one substantive defect is Q21, whose key contradicts the standard shell result and must be rewritten; the remaining fixes are wording clarifications in Q4 and Q15.

[minor] "Floats across two immiscible liquid layers" is unidiomatic and the stem never states that the remaining 25% of the volume lies above the upper liquid (in air), which the intended solution silently assumes; reword as "floats at the interface of two immiscible liquids, with 50% of its volume in the lower liquid, 25% in the upper liquid and the rest in air."

[minor] "A square loop ... is placed perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field" is ambiguous (plane perpendicular to B versus plane containing B); specify "with its plane perpendicular to the field" so the flux 0.5 × 0.04 Wb is unambiguous.

[major] The key is wrong: inside a uniform shell the field is zero and the potential is the constant −GM/R, independent of the test mass m, so option (B) is indefensible and only (A) can be keyed (it should read "V depends on M and R"), and the phrase "at any other point inside the shell" should be dropped.
[minor] The thermometer-in-a-water-bath framing is irrelevant padding for a bare one-step Celsius-to-Fahrenheit conversion that sits below the difficulty of the rest of the section.

Chemistry: All forty keys check out, the numerical data are consistent (Hess's law, Ksp, Nernst, kinetics and colligative items all give the stated answers), and coverage across physical, inorganic and organic chemistry is broad and syllabus-appropriate. The level is on the easy side for BITSAT: most items are single-fact recall or one-step substitutions, with only Q48, Q68 and Q69 demanding real multi-step work, so adding one or two genuinely reasoning-based items would improve discrimination. The only structural weakness is the repeated VSEPR geometry testing in Q42/Q59 with overlapping option sets, plus a couple of small wording imprecisions.

[minor] This item resolves by the same VSEPR lone-pair/geometry analysis as Q42 and reuses two of its options (NF₃, ClF₃), so swap in a different molecule set (e.g. CO₂, BF₃, CCl₄, SO₂) to avoid near-duplication within the section.
[minor] "Arrange the ions" is ambiguous because each half-reaction lists both M³⁺ and M²⁺; state explicitly "arrange the divalent ions (M²⁺) in decreasing order of reducing strength".

[minor] Rinsing with titrant is done before filling, not "during the titration", and the strong-acid/strong-base detail is irrelevant; reword to "Before filling the burette, it is rinsed with the titrant after washing with water, in order to…".

English Proficiency: All fifteen keys are correct and unambiguous, and the difficulty level is appropriate for BITSAT, with a clean, well-written comprehension passage and sensible distractors elsewhere. The main imbalance is grammatical error-spotting, which occupies four of the fifteen slots (81, 83, 86, 89) while synonyms and antonyms get only one each; converting one error item into a vocabulary or comprehension question would give better coverage. Two items also carry type labels that do not match their actual content and should be retagged before printing.

[minor] The item is tagged "Sentence Completion (vocabulary)" but is actually a spelling question, and the stem asks for "the correct spelling of the word" without ever naming the word — retag it as spelling and name the target word (surveillance) or reword the stem to "select the correctly spelt word".
[minor] The item is tagged "Sentence Completion (vocabulary)" although it is a word-analogy item with no blank to fill, so the type label should be corrected to "Analogies".

Logical Reasoning: The section covers the expected BITSAT logical-reasoning spread (folding, classification, blood relations, dictionary order, syllogism, series, figure puzzle, analogy, coding) with no two items testing the same skill, and keys for the nine text-verifiable items are all correct. Difficulty is appropriate — most items are 30–60 s solves, with the number series and paper-folding items providing the only real stretch, so the level is slightly easy but acceptable. Only the coding–decoding item needs rewriting with a transparent, single-example-deducible rule; the three figure-based items should be checked against their artwork before printing.

[major] The single example GARDEN → 313991 fits no deducible coding rule (e.g., digit-sums of alphabet positions give 719455), and the letter A maps to 1 in GARDEN but to 2 in the keyed PLANET code 382894, so the vague "letter-and-position rule" cannot be recovered and key A is unverifiable.

Mathematics: All forty-five keys verify correctly and the topic spread (algebra, coordinate geometry, 3-D/vectors, calculus, probability and statistics) matches the BITSAT pattern with a reasonable easy-to-moderate gradient. The difficulty curve is uneven at the top end, where Q118 and Q125 demand multi-case or multi-step work that cannot be completed in about 90 seconds, while Q143 and Q145 sit at bare-recall level. Replacing the two over-long computations with shorter application items and swapping the duplicated independence question would give a well-balanced section.

[major] Although the key 7/64 is correct, evaluating this integral needs rationalising the cube (or the non-obvious substitution t = √(x²+2) − x) followed by integrating (4x²+2)√(x²+2) and a cubic, which is well beyond the ~90-second budget.

[major] The count 752 is right, but it requires roughly six sub-cases (0 or 5 as the repeated digit vs. a single digit, each with the leading-zero restriction), making the item far too long and error-prone for a 90-second slot.

[minor] This tests the same P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B) independence check already examined in Q129; replace it with a different probability skill (e.g. total probability/Bayes or expectation) to avoid duplication.
[minor] "Any nonempty selection of 5 distinct fruit types" can be read as selecting all five; change to "selection from 5 distinct fruit types" (the item is otherwise a trivial 2⁵−1 recall).
[minor] Pure definitional recall of the focus–directrix property that is already the working principle of Q106, so it is both too trivial and conceptually redundant here.
